questions.question: What would Leila probably say about the restaurant?
options: a) 'It's easy for us because everyone shares the work.'
b) 'I can't wait to take it over from my parents when I'm older.'
c) 'It's very hard work, but I admire my parents for doing it.'
d) 'My parents should have stayed in their safe jobs.'
questions.explanation: Leila says running the business 'is not always easy' and that she has 'seen how tiring it is', but also: 'I'm proud of what my parents have done.' She does not want to run a restaurant herself ('I don't think I want to run a restaurant myself one day'), and she understands 'why they gave up safe jobs', so she does not think they should have stayed.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (1)?
options: A) Instead, volunteers built raised beds, which are large wooden boxes filled with soil.
B) Luckily, the ground there was already soft and easy to dig.
C) When one neighbour was in hospital last winter, for example, others took turns to cook for her family.
D) So she knocked on every door in the street to ask her neighbours what they thought.
E) Sadly, the garden had to close after only one summer.
F) The children there have been growing their own strawberries, and they are very proud of them.
G) During that time, the group raised money by selling cakes and second-hand books.
H) Unfortunately, almost every neighbour she spoke to was against the idea.
questions.explanation: Priya 'thought what a waste it was', 'So she knocked on every door in the street to ask her neighbours what they thought.' The next sentence, 'Most of them liked the idea', needs 'her neighbours' as the people who answered. The sentence saying almost every neighbour was against the idea cannot go here, because the text says 'Most of them liked the idea'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (2)?
options: A) Instead, volunteers built raised beds, which are large wooden boxes filled with soil.
B) Luckily, the ground there was already soft and easy to dig.
C) When one neighbour was in hospital last winter, for example, others took turns to cook for her family.
D) So she knocked on every door in the street to ask her neighbours what they thought.
E) Sadly, the garden had to close after only one summer.
F) The children there have been growing their own strawberries, and they are very proud of them.
G) During that time, the group raised money by selling cakes and second-hand books.
H) Unfortunately, almost every neighbour she spoke to was against the idea.
questions.explanation: 'During that time' refers to the year it 'took almost a year' to get permission, and raising money explains the next sentence: 'By the time the council finally said yes, they had enough to buy wood, soil and tools.' Without this sentence, 'they had enough' has nothing to refer to.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (3)?
options: A) Instead, volunteers built raised beds, which are large wooden boxes filled with soil.
B) Luckily, the ground there was already soft and easy to dig.
C) When one neighbour was in hospital last winter, for example, others took turns to cook for her family.
D) So she knocked on every door in the street to ask her neighbours what they thought.
E) Sadly, the garden had to close after only one summer.
F) The children there have been growing their own strawberries, and they are very proud of them.
G) During that time, the group raised money by selling cakes and second-hand books.
H) Unfortunately, almost every neighbour she spoke to was against the idea.
questions.explanation: 'Nothing could be planted directly in it', so 'Instead, volunteers built raised beds'. The raised beds explain why older members 'can now reach their plants without bending down'. The sentence about soft ground that was 'easy to dig' contradicts 'the ground was concrete'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (4)?
options: A) Instead, volunteers built raised beds, which are large wooden boxes filled with soil.
B) Luckily, the ground there was already soft and easy to dig.
C) When one neighbour was in hospital last winter, for example, others took turns to cook for her family.
D) So she knocked on every door in the street to ask her neighbours what they thought.
E) Sadly, the garden had to close after only one summer.
F) The children there have been growing their own strawberries, and they are very proud of them.
G) During that time, the group raised money by selling cakes and second-hand books.
H) Unfortunately, almost every neighbour she spoke to was against the idea.
questions.explanation: 'The children there' are the pupils of the 'local primary school' that uses the garden as 'an outdoor classroom'. Growing strawberries links to the next sentence: 'Their teacher says that some pupils who never ate fruit at home now ask for it.' The sentence saying the garden closed cannot fit, because the text says 'Today, the garden is open to anyone.'

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (5)?
options: A) Instead, volunteers built raised beds, which are large wooden boxes filled with soil.
B) Luckily, the ground there was already soft and easy to dig.
C) When one neighbour was in hospital last winter, for example, others took turns to cook for her family.
D) So she knocked on every door in the street to ask her neighbours what they thought.
E) Sadly, the garden had to close after only one summer.
F) The children there have been growing their own strawberries, and they are very proud of them.
G) During that time, the group raised money by selling cakes and second-hand books.
H) Unfortunately, almost every neighbour she spoke to was against the idea.
questions.explanation: Priya says 'Now they really know each other', and this sentence gives an example ('for example') of neighbours helping each other: 'others took turns to cook for her family'. The sentence about neighbours being against the idea belongs to the start of the project, not to how people get on now, and it contradicts 'Most of them liked the idea'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (1).
options: a) explained
b) said
c) suggested
d) advised
questions.explanation: The text says Mr Hughes "advised us to wear light clothes": the verb is followed by an object and 'to' + infinitive. 'Said', 'suggested' and 'explained' cannot be used in the pattern 'verb + us + to do' (we say 'suggested that we wear', 'explained that…').

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (2).
options: a) looked
b) noticed
c) showed
d) pointed
questions.explanation: The guide "pointed out a small green frog": 'point out' means to show something to someone so they see it. 'Showed out' and 'noticed out' are not phrasal verbs, and 'looked out' means 'be careful', which does not fit with an object like 'a small green frog'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (3).
options: a) breath
b) air
c) voice
d) breeze
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "hold our breath": the students stayed completely still and quiet "in case we frightened them". English does not say 'hold our air', 'hold our voice' or 'hold our breeze'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (4).
options: a) make
b) do
c) play
d) give
questions.explanation: The collocation is "play an important part in" something: rainforests "play an important part in keeping our planet healthy". We do not say 'make', 'do' or 'give an important part in'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (5).
options: a) put
b) did
c) made
d) gave
questions.explanation: Students "did a short quiz" and then the writer says "I got nine out of ten", so they answered the quiz. In English you do a quiz when you answer the questions. If you make or give a quiz, you write it or set it for other people, and you cannot put a quiz.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (6).
options: a) took
b) made
c) got
d) brought
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "take someone by surprise": the good result "really took me by surprise". 'Made', 'got' and 'brought me by surprise' are not English expressions.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: "Before that trip, neither of us had ever slept in a tent": the past perfect (had + past participle 'slept') is needed for an experience before another past time. 'Has' is wrong because the story is in the past, and 'did' cannot go before 'slept'.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: After a comparative adjective we use 'than': "much smaller than it looked in the photo online".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes after an adjective and is followed by 'for': "it wasn't big enough for both of us", so they "left them in the car". 'Too' and 'very' go before the adjective, not after it.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: 'Own' must follow a possessive adjective, and the raincoat belongs to Freya: "she had left her own raincoat at home". 'My' is impossible because she then had "to borrow mine".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (5).
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'such + a + adjective + noun + that': "It was such a cold night that we slept in our jumpers". 'So' cannot go before 'a cold night' (we say 'so cold that').

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'take off' means remove clothes or shoes: because "mud got everywhere", they "took off our boots before climbing into the tent".

questions.question:
Part 1. You must answer this question.

Read this email from your classmate Priya and the notes you have made.

From: Priya
Subject: Our science project

Hi!

I'm really happy we're doing the science project together. Mr Evans says we can choose between two topics: 'Plastic in the sea' or 'Saving energy at home'. Which one do you prefer? [Note 1: Say which and why]

We need to meet to work on it before the end of next week. When are you free? [Note 2: Tell Priya]

We also have to make a poster to go with our talk. I'm not very good at drawing, so what could we do? [Note 3: Suggest …]

Oh, and we have to give the talk in front of the whole class. I get really nervous when I speak in public! [Note 4: Give Priya some advice]

See you soon,
Priya

Write your email to Priya using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: A good answer is a friendly email (e.g. 'Hi Priya,' … 'See you soon,') of about 100 words that deals with all four notes: (1) chooses one of the two topics and gives a reason ('I'd prefer Saving energy at home because we can do experiments in our own houses'); (2) says when the writer is free ('I'm free on Tuesday after school or on Thursday afternoon'); (3) makes a suggestion about the poster ('We could use photos from the internet' / 'Why don't we ask my brother? He draws really well'); (4) gives advice about speaking in public ('Try to practise the talk at home first' / 'Don't worry, I'll speak first'). Marks are given for Content (all four notes answered), Communicative Achievement (friendly, informal tone suitable for a classmate), Organisation (clear paragraphs, linking words such as 'because', 'also', 'so') and Language (a range of B1 vocabulary and structures, e.g. 'I'd prefer', 'Why don't we…?', 'You should…'). An answer that misses a note cannot get full marks for Content.

questions.question:
Part 2. Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2: Article
You see this notice in an English-language magazine for young people.

ARTICLES WANTED!
Something new I learned this year
What new thing did you learn this year? How did you learn it? Why was it important to you?
Write an article answering these questions. We will publish the best articles in next month's magazine.

Write your article.

Question 3: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
'The teacher smiled and handed me the results.'

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Candidates answer only ONE question, in about 100 words. Article: a good answer has a title, catches the reader's interest (e.g. a question to the reader), and answers all three questions in the notice: what was learned (e.g. how to cook, a new language, a musical instrument), how (from a course, a family member, online videos) and why it mattered (it made the writer more confident, helped the family). It should express personal opinions and feelings ('I was surprised how…', 'The best thing was…'). Story: the story must begin with the given sentence and continue logically from it (what the results were, how the writer felt, what happened next). It needs a clear beginning, middle and end, past tenses used correctly (past simple, past continuous, past perfect where possible), and linking words for sequence ('At first', 'Then', 'In the end'). Both are marked for Content, Communicative Achievement, Organisation and Language.

questions.question:
Part 1 (2-3 minutes). The examiner asks you some questions about yourself.

What's your name? Where do you live?
How do you usually get to school or work?
How long does the journey take?
Do you prefer travelling by bus or by train? Why?
Tell us about a place you would like to visit in the future.
What did you do on your last holiday?
questions.explanation: Answer each question with more than one or two words: give a short answer and then add a reason or an example. For instance: 'I usually go to school by bike because it's only ten minutes from my house, and it's good exercise.' Use the present simple for routines ('I usually take the bus'), 'would like to' for wishes ('I'd like to visit Japan because…') and the past simple for your last holiday ('We went to the coast and stayed in a small hotel'). The examiner assesses Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management (extending answers), Pronunciation and Interactive Communication.

questions.question: Part 2 (about 1 minute). Look at the photograph. It shows some people at a busy train station. A family with suitcases is waiting on the platform next to a train, and other people are looking up at a board with the train times. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.
questions.explanation: Talk on your own for about one minute. Describe the place ('This photo was taken at a train station, probably in a big city'), the people and what they are doing, using the present continuous ('A family is waiting on the platform', 'Some people are looking at the board'). Mention details such as clothes, luggage and the weather or time of day, and guess about the situation ('I think they are going on holiday because they have got big suitcases'). Useful language: 'In the foreground / background', 'on the left / right', 'It looks like…', 'Maybe they're…'. If you don't know a word, explain it in other words ('the thing you pull your bags on'). Do not stop after a few sentences: keep talking until the examiner says thank you.

questions.question:
Part 3 (2-3 minutes). Talk to your partner.

A group of students from another country is visiting your town for one day. Here are some things they could do during their visit:

visit the town museum
take a boat trip on the river
go shopping in the town centre
have a picnic in the park
go on a bike tour of the town
visit the old castle

Talk together about the different things the students could do, and say which would be the most interesting for them.
questions.explanation: This is a conversation with your partner, not a speech. Talk about each idea in turn, give your opinion with a reason and ask your partner what they think: 'I think a boat trip would be great because they can see the whole town from the river. What do you think?' Agree and disagree politely ('That's a good idea, but…', 'I'm not sure about that because…') and make suggestions ('What about…?', 'Why don't they…?'). Near the end, try to reach a decision together: 'So, shall we choose the bike tour?' You do not have to agree, but you must discuss the options and try to decide. The examiner assesses how well you keep the conversation going and respond to your partner.

questions.question:
Part 4 (about 3 minutes). The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about transport and holidays.

What do you like to do when you visit a new place?
Do you prefer going on holiday in your own country or abroad? Why?
What is the best way to travel around your town?
Do you think people use their cars too much? Why / Why not?
Would you like to go on a long journey by train? Why / Why not?
questions.explanation: Give full answers with reasons and examples, and react to what your partner says ('I agree with you, and also…', 'That's interesting. For me…'). For example: 'I prefer holidays abroad because I love trying new food and hearing other languages, but they can be expensive.' For opinion questions, use phrases such as 'In my opinion…', 'I think that…', 'On the other hand…'. Use 'would' for imaginary situations ('I'd love to go across Europe by train because you can see a lot of different places'). The examiner assesses range of language, extending answers and interaction with your partner.

questions.question: Which job does the man want Ollie to do first?
options: a) wash the car
b) tidy his bedroom
c) cut the long grass
questions.explanation: The man says Ollie's bedroom "looks terrible" and tells him "start with that, please". The car washing "can wait until tomorrow", and the grass is "too wet to cut today".

questions.question: Where did Jenny find her keys?
options: a) by the washing machine
b) in the pocket of her coat
c) in the garden shed
questions.explanation: Jenny says "They were by the washing machine!" She looked in her coat pocket and went to the garden shed, but the keys were not in either place.

questions.question: What is Paul going to buy at the garden centre?
options: a) some red flowers
b) a new spade
c) some grass seed
questions.explanation: Paul says he is going "because the handle's broken on the spade" and "it's just the spade". He bought flowers "last week", and they still have "half a box" of grass seed.

questions.question: How long did it take Mia to paint her room?
options: a) a week
b) two days
c) three days
questions.explanation: Mia says "I finished on Monday after school. Three days altogether." Two days was only her plan, and "a week" is how long the man took to paint the kitchen.

questions.question: What does Mrs Patel need someone to repair?
options: a) the tap
b) the fridge
c) the kitchen window
questions.explanation: Mrs Patel says "This time it's the tap. It won't turn off properly". The window was fixed last month, and the fridge is "not urgent" because "it's still keeping things cold".

questions.question: What does Josh's grandmother want him to help with?
options: a) cutting the hedge
b) picking apples
c) moving some pots
questions.explanation: Gran says the big pots "are much too heavy for me now" and she wants "to move them into the greenhouse". She has already picked the apples herself, and Mr Lewis "has offered to cut the hedge".

questions.question: What does Kate ask Rob to do this evening?
options: a) iron her blue shirt
b) take out the rubbish
c) do all the washing-up
questions.explanation: Kate asks "could you take the bins out before you go to bed?" because "tomorrow's rubbish day". She will do the washing-up herself "when I get back", and she says "No, thanks" to the ironing.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a new restaurant. What does Jess think of it?
options: a) The prices are too high for what you get.
b) The service is not as good as the food.
c) The meals are too small.
questions.explanation: Jess loved the pasta ("the best I've had in this town"), but "we waited forty minutes" and "the waiter got our drinks wrong twice". She agrees it is cheap ("It is") and says "you get loads on your plate".

questions.question: You will hear a boy talking to his father. Why does the boy want to cook dinner?
options: a) To show his father a recipe
b) To practise for a competition
c) To surprise his mother on her birthday
questions.explanation: Finn explains "We've got a cooking competition in two weeks" and "I want to try my recipe at home first and see how long it takes". His mother's birthday is "next month", so it isn't a surprise for her.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about vegetarian food. What do they agree about?
options: a) It can cost less than meat.
b) It is always healthier than meat.
c) Restaurants have plenty of good vegetarian dishes.
questions.explanation: Nadia says "my shopping costs much less" and Callum answers "That’s true." Callum is "not sure it’s always healthier", and Nadia complains that "Most places only have one boring vegetarian dish".

questions.question: You will hear a woman telling a friend about a cooking class. What was she disappointed with?
options: a) The other people in the group
b) How difficult the recipes were to follow
c) The way the chef taught the class
questions.explanation: Helen says the chef "just stood at the front reading from his notes" and "didn't come round once", and "I won't do another class with him." The recipes were "really easy", and "The other people were lovely".

questions.question: You will hear a girl talking to her grandfather about a family recipe. What does she want to do?
options: a) Sell the cakes at a school fair
b) Make some changes to the original recipe
c) Keep a written copy of the recipe
questions.explanation: Isla says "I’ll write everything down as we go, so it’s never lost" and "I just don’t want the recipe to disappear." Selling cakes is Grandad’s idea, and she only answers "Maybe one day!"

questions.question: You will hear two flatmates talking about food shopping. What does Joe suggest?
options: a) Doing the shopping online
b) Going to the supermarket more often
c) Writing a shopping list
questions.explanation: Joe says "Why don't we just order everything on the internet once a week?" The list was Becky's idea, and Joe rejects it: "We tried that, remember? Nobody looked at it."

questions.question: Accommodation this year: all students will stay with ____.
questions.explanation: Richard says the college rooms 'are being repaired this year, so everyone will be living with host families'. The college rooms were used in the past, so they are not the answer.

questions.question: Number of lessons each morning: ____
questions.explanation: Richard says 'There are four lessons each morning'. Fifty is the number of minutes each lesson lasts, not the number of lessons.

questions.question: Most popular afternoon activity: ____
questions.explanation: Richard says 'Many students expect football to be the favourite, but in fact drama is always the most popular.' Football is only what students expect.

questions.question: This year's first Saturday trip: a visit to a ____ on the coast.
questions.explanation: Richard says 'this year we're starting with a visit to a castle on the coast'. The museum in Leeds was last year's first trip.

questions.question: Students should remember to pack a ____.
questions.explanation: Richard says 'please do pack a raincoat', because the weather 'can change very quickly'. Towels and sheets are not needed, because host families provide them.

questions.question: Students receive their certificates at a ____ in the school garden.
questions.explanation: Richard says 'we hold a party in the school garden, and that's when you'll receive your certificate'.

questions.question: Why did Daniel decide to become a vet?
options: a) He saw a vet save an animal on a farm.
b) He had loved animals since he was very small.
c) He was good at science subjects at school.
questions.explanation: Daniel describes the night on his uncle's farm when 'The vet arrived, and an hour later the mother and the calf were both fine', and says 'that's what I want to do.' He was good at science, but at that time he 'wanted to be an engineer', and as a child he was 'frightened of dogs'.

questions.question: What surprised Daniel when he started working as a vet?
options: a) How many hours he had to work each day
b) How hard the studying at university had been
c) How much he had to talk to owners
questions.explanation: Daniel says 'What I hadn't expected was how much of the job is talking to people.' He says he 'was ready for' the hard studying and 'knew the hours would be long', so neither surprised him.

questions.question: What does Daniel enjoy most about his job?
options: a) Working outside on farms
b) Carrying out operations
c) Seeing young animals at the practice
questions.explanation: Daniel says 'what I really enjoy is driving out to the farms and being outside, even when it's pouring with rain.' He says puppies are 'lovely' and operations 'can be exciting', but neither is what he enjoys most.

questions.question: How does Daniel feel about working at night?
options: a) He hopes he can stop doing it soon.
b) He accepts it, although it is tiring.
c) He prefers it to working during the day.
questions.explanation: Daniel says 'I'm often very tired the next day. But it's part of being a vet, and I accept that.' He finds some night work 'quite special', but he never says he prefers it to daytime work.

questions.question: What does Daniel think about owners who look for information online?
options: a) He finds it annoying, like his colleagues.
b) It frightens them more than it should.
c) They often know as much as some vets do.
questions.explanation: Daniel says owners 'often read about the worst possible illness, so they arrive much more worried than they need to be.' He says 'Some of my colleagues get quite annoyed, but I don't.'

questions.question: What does Daniel say about his plans for the future?
options: a) He is thinking of moving to a city.
b) He would like to open his own practice.
c) He hopes to teach students one day.
questions.explanation: Daniel says 'What I would like, though, is to teach vet students part-time one day.' His friends have opened practices in the city, but he says 'I'm really happy where I am' and running a business 'doesn't appeal to me at all'.

questions.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) Members pay less for early films on Tuesdays.
b) Any customer can see a film for £5 on Tuesdays.
c) New members get a free ticket when they join.
questions.explanation: On Tuesdays 'Members can see any film starting before 6 pm for just £5', so early films are cheaper for members. The £5 price is for members, not any customer, and people who join get 'a free drink with every ticket you buy', not a free ticket.

questions.question: What does Leah want Sophie to do?
options: a) Email her a copy of her ticket
b) Go into the cinema without her
c) Wait for her outside the entrance
questions.explanation: Leah writes 'Don't wait for me outside … go in and find our seats', so Sophie should go in alone. Leah has already emailed Sophie her ticket; she does not ask Sophie to send her one.

questions.question: What does the sign say about people who arrive late?
options: a) They cannot go to their seats straight away.
b) They must stay in the bar for the second half.
c) They will not be able to see any of the show.
questions.explanation: Latecomers 'will be able to take [their] seat during the interval, about 50 minutes later', so they have to wait before going in. They can see the first part 'on a screen in the theatre bar', and after the interval they go to their seats, so they do not stay in the bar.

questions.question: Why has the theatre written to Mr Brennan?
options: a) To offer him free tickets for next week
b) To ask him to make a choice
c) To tell him another actor will play the main part
questions.explanation: Mr Brennan can 'either change [his] tickets … or get [his] money back' and must 'reply to tell us which you prefer', so he has to choose. The performance is cancelled, so no other actor will play the part, and the new tickets are for 'another night this week', not free tickets for next week.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) You have to buy all your drinks at the cinema.
b) Food from the cinema café is not allowed in the screens.
c) You can take water from home into the screens.
questions.explanation: Food and drinks from outside are not allowed, but 'Bottles of water are the only exception', so you can bring water in. This means you do not have to buy every drink at the cinema, and the rule is about food bought outside the cinema, not food from the cinema itself.

questions.question: Ryan is 15 and has never played in a team, but he'd like to try a team sport. He can only train after school on weekdays.
options: A) Riverside Rowing Club
B) Summit Climbing Team
C) Aqua Fit at Parkway Pool
D) Northside Basketball Club
E) Westfield Youth Football Academy
F) Sunrise Fitness Group
G) Peak Climbing Wall
H) Balance Pilates Studio
questions.explanation: Northside Basketball Club has 'junior teams', 'Complete beginners are very welcome', and training is 'on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 4.30 to 6 pm'. Westfield Youth Football Academy is also a team sport for his age, but players 'must … have played for a club for at least a year' and training is on Saturdays.

questions.question: Anita wants to get fitter by exercising outdoors with other people before she goes to work. She doesn't enjoy competition and just wants to have a good time.
options: A) Riverside Rowing Club
B) Summit Climbing Team
C) Aqua Fit at Parkway Pool
D) Northside Basketball Club
E) Westfield Youth Football Academy
F) Sunrise Fitness Group
G) Peak Climbing Wall
H) Balance Pilates Studio
questions.explanation: Sunrise Fitness Group meets 'in Victoria Park at 6.30 every weekday morning', 'there are no races or times to beat' and 'It's all about having fun together'. Riverside Rowing Club also trains outdoors early in the morning, but it is for people 'who are serious about competing'.

questions.question: Lukas has a bad back, and his doctor has told him to try a gentle form of exercise. He works long hours during the week, so he wants an indoor class at the weekend.
options: A) Riverside Rowing Club
B) Summit Climbing Team
C) Aqua Fit at Parkway Pool
D) Northside Basketball Club
E) Westfield Youth Football Academy
F) Sunrise Fitness Group
G) Peak Climbing Wall
H) Balance Pilates Studio
questions.explanation: At Balance Pilates Studio 'many doctors recommend it for people with back pain', the classes are 'indoor', and they are 'on Saturday and Sunday mornings'. Aqua Fit is also gentle and good for 'problems with your back', but it only runs on weekdays at lunchtime.

questions.question: Grace and her ten-year-old daughter are looking for a new activity that they can learn together. Saturday is the only day they are both free.
options: A) Riverside Rowing Club
B) Summit Climbing Team
C) Aqua Fit at Parkway Pool
D) Northside Basketball Club
E) Westfield Youth Football Academy
F) Sunrise Fitness Group
G) Peak Climbing Wall
H) Balance Pilates Studio
questions.explanation: Peak Climbing Wall has 'family sessions' on 'Saturday mornings, where parents and children aged eight and over learn to climb side by side'. Westfield Youth Football Academy also trains on Saturday mornings, but it is only for young players aged 14 to 18, so Grace could not take part.

questions.question: Tomasz has been climbing for many years and now wants to see how good he is compared with other climbers. He would also love to climb abroad.
options: A) Riverside Rowing Club
B) Summit Climbing Team
C) Aqua Fit at Parkway Pool
D) Northside Basketball Club
E) Westfield Youth Football Academy
F) Sunrise Fitness Group
G) Peak Climbing Wall
H) Balance Pilates Studio
questions.explanation: Summit Climbing Team is for people who 'want to test themselves against others', members 'take part in regional and national competitions', and there is a summer 'trip to climb in the mountains of Spain or France'. Peak Climbing Wall is also for climbing, but it offers 'beginners' courses' and family sessions, not competitions or trips abroad.

questions.question: Why does Isla walk round every enclosure at the start of the day?
options: a) To spend some time playing with the animals
b) To notice if any animal might have a problem
c) To check that all the gates are safely locked
d) To give the animals their first meal of the day
questions.explanation: Isla says 'You learn to notice small things, like an otter that isn't eating', and 'If something seems wrong, I write it down and tell the vet.' Feeding comes later ('Then I prepare the food'), and she says keepers do not play with the animals: 'we try not to touch them much'. Gates are not mentioned.

questions.question: Why do the keepers try not to touch the animals much?
options: a) So that the animals behave as they would in the wild
b) Because visitors are not supposed to see it happen
c) Because some of the animals could be dangerous
d) So that diseases cannot pass from one animal to another
questions.explanation: Isla explains: 'They're wild animals, not pets, and we want them to behave as naturally as possible.' Stopping diseases is the reason she gives for cleaning ('a clean enclosure stops diseases from spreading'), not for avoiding touching. She never says the animals are dangerous or mentions visitors seeing it.

questions.question: What is Isla's attitude to the cleaning she does?
options: a) She feels it takes up too much of her morning.
b) She enjoys it more than preparing the food.
c) She accepts it because it keeps the animals healthy.
d) She thinks it is the most tiring part of her job.
questions.explanation: She says: 'It isn't exciting, but a clean enclosure stops diseases from spreading, so I don't mind it.' She spends 'at least two hours' on it but does not complain about the time. What hurts her back is 'lifting heavy bags of food', not cleaning, and she does not compare it with preparing food.

questions.question: How did Isla become better at giving talks?
options: a) She asked children to send in their questions.
b) She practised her script many more times.
c) She started telling stories about the animals.
d) She watched the other keepers giving talks.
questions.explanation: 'My manager suggested I forget the script and simply tell people stories about the animals instead. That changed everything.' Learning the script by heart was what she did before, when her talks were 'a disaster'. Children's questions are something she enjoys now, not how she improved.

questions.question: What might Isla write in a message to a friend?
options: a) 'This is exactly the job I dreamed about when I was little.'
b) 'I'm going back to college soon to train as a vet.'
c) 'I'm glad I failed my exams because I never wanted to be a vet.'
d) 'It's badly paid and hard on my body, but I love it.'
questions.explanation: Isla says 'I'm not paid much, and my back often hurts', but she 'wouldn't change this job for anything'. As a child she 'wanted to be a vet', so this was not her childhood dream, and she 'was disappointed' about her results, so she was not glad. Nothing suggests she plans to go back to college.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (1)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'Places like this' refers to The Dice Box, and 'Ten years ago, however' contrasts with the next sentence: 'Today there are more than five hundred across the country.' The sentence saying most customers prefer to play on their phones contradicts 'hardly anyone is looking at a phone'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (2)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'So many on the shelves' refers to 'a library of over 800 games', and the problem that 'newcomers often have no idea where to start' explains the next sentence: 'That is why the café employs game guides… to recommend a game.' The sentence about the café stopping buying games has no cause here and does not lead to game guides.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (3)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'They' refers to the 'People' who spend 'all day looking at a computer at work', and sitting 'round a real table with real people' is what 'that' means in Tom's next words: 'A screen can never give them that.' The sentence about Tom learning chess does not continue his quote and gives 'that' nothing to refer to.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (4)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'One of them' refers to the 'group of retired teachers', and introducing Margaret explains who 'she' is in the next sentence: 'I play against my grandchildren now… she laughs.' The sentence about Tom learning chess cannot fit, because the next speaker is a woman with grandchildren.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (5)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'To stop this happening' refers to 'small pieces often go missing', and checking every box is what 'It takes time' describes; Tom adds that 'A game with one card missing is a game nobody can finish.' The sentence about stopping buying new games does not explain what 'takes time' or why a missing card matters.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (1).
options: a) clear
b) take
c) carry
d) keep
questions.explanation: The family helped Gran "clear out her old house", which means empty it and remove the things she no longer needed before moving. 'Take out' is not used with a house as the object in this meaning, 'carry out' means 'do a task' (carry out an experiment), and 'keep out' means 'stay outside', which is the opposite of helping.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (2).
options: a) discover
b) realise
c) notice
d) recognise
questions.explanation: Gran looked at the faces and "a few she couldn't recognise at all": she did not know who those people were. 'Notice' and 'discover' do not fit because the people were right in front of her in the photos, and 'realise' needs a fact (realise that…), not a person.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (3).
options: a) bake
b) boil
c) fry
d) roast
questions.explanation: Gran worked in "a bakery", and bread is cooked in an oven, so she got up early "to bake the bread". Bread is not boiled, fried or roasted.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (4).
options: a) behaviour
b) health
c) condition
d) mood
questions.explanation: Objects can be "in quite bad condition" when they are damaged: here "water had got into the box". 'Health', 'mood' and 'behaviour' describe people (or animals), not photographs.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (5).
options: a) under
b) behind
c) between
d) along
questions.explanation: "The stories behind them" means the true events that explain the photos, for example how Gran came to work at the bakery. 'The stories under / between / along them' make no sense here.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (6).
options: a) make
b) do
c) put
d) get
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "get in touch with" someone, meaning to contact them: Callum "hopes to get in touch with some of our distant cousins". We do not say 'make', 'do' or 'put in touch with' about contacting people ourselves.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: This is a non-defining relative clause between commas about a person: "Mr Okafor, who has written several plays himself, gave me the role". 'That' cannot be used after a comma in this kind of clause, and 'which' is for things.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'learn something by heart', meaning learn it so you can say it from memory: "two hundred lines to learn by heart".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: 'Had better' + infinitive without 'to' gives strong advice or a warning: "You had better start learning them today, or you won't be ready," Mr Okafor warned. Only 'had' can go before 'better' here; 'would', 'should' or 'must' + 'better' are not possible.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: 'Each other' shows that people do the same thing to one another: the cast "helped each other with difficult scenes".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (5).
questions.explanation: A superlative with a long adjective is 'the most + adjective', often with 'I have ever been': "I was the most nervous I have ever been". 'Least' is impossible because "my hands were shaking and my mouth was completely dry".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: 'As soon as' is a time conjunction meaning 'immediately when': "as soon as the curtain went up … my nerves disappeared". 'As long as' and 'as far as' have different meanings that do not fit here.

questions.question:
Part 1. You must answer this question.

Read this email from your friend Callum and the notes you have made.

From: Callum
Subject: Concert tickets!

Guess what? I've got two tickets for the Silver Foxes concert at the City Arena on Saturday 14 June! [Note 1: Great!]

The concert starts at eight o'clock in the evening. How do you think we should get there? [Note 2: Suggest …]

Shall we have something to eat in town before the concert? [Note 3: Yes, because …]

There's one problem. My sister Jess really wants to come with us, but all the tickets have gone. What should I say to her? [Note 4: Explain]

Talk soon,
Callum

Write your email to Callum using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: A good answer is an informal email to a friend (e.g. 'Hi Callum,' … 'See you on Saturday!') of about 100 words that deals with all four notes: (1) reacts with enthusiasm to the tickets ('That's amazing news! The Silver Foxes are my favourite band'); (2) suggests a way to travel ('Let's take the bus, because it stops right outside the arena' / 'My dad could drive us'); (3) agrees to eat before the concert and gives a reason ('Yes, good idea, because we'll be hungry by ten o'clock'); (4) explains what Callum could tell his sister ('You could tell Jess that we'll take lots of videos for her' / 'Maybe we can all go together next time'). Marks are given for Content (all four notes), Communicative Achievement (friendly, natural tone), Organisation (clear paragraphs and linking words such as 'because', 'so', 'but') and Language (B1 structures such as 'Let's…', 'could', 'will' for plans and offers). Missing a note reduces the Content mark.

questions.question:
Part 2. Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2: Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

ARTICLES WANTED!
The best concert or show I have seen
What was the concert or show? Who did you go with? Why was it so special?
Write an article answering these questions. The best articles will appear on our website.

Write your article.

Question 3: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
'The lights went out just before the show started.'

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Candidates answer only ONE question, in about 100 words. Article: a good answer has a title and an interesting opening, and answers the three questions in the notice: which concert or show (a band, a musical, a dance show, a school performance), who the writer went with, and why it was special (the atmosphere, the music, a surprise moment). It should describe feelings and give opinions ('It was the most exciting evening of my life'), and may use superlatives and adjectives such as 'amazing', 'unforgettable'. Story: the story must begin with the given sentence and develop it (why the lights went out, what the audience and the writer did, how the problem was solved). It needs a clear beginning, middle and end, a range of past tenses (e.g. 'Everyone was waiting when…'), and sequencing words ('Suddenly', 'After a few minutes', 'Finally'). Both are marked for Content, Communicative Achievement, Organisation and Language.

questions.question:
Part 1 (2-3 minutes). The examiner asks you some questions about yourself.

What's your name? How old are you?
What sports do you like doing?
How often do you do some exercise?
Do you prefer playing sport or watching it? Why?
Tell us about a sport you would like to try.
What sports did you do at primary school?
questions.explanation: Answer each question with a short answer and then add a reason or an example: 'I go swimming twice a week, usually on Mondays and Thursdays, because there's a pool near my flat.' Use adverbs of frequency for routines ('I often play basketball'), 'would like to' for wishes ('I'd like to try surfing because it looks exciting') and the past simple for things you did as a child ('We played a lot of football at primary school'). The examiner assesses Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management (extending answers), Pronunciation and Interactive Communication.

questions.question: Part 2 (about 1 minute). Look at the photograph. It shows a group of young people playing volleyball on a beach on a sunny day. Some of them are jumping to hit the ball, and a few friends are sitting on towels and watching. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.
questions.explanation: Talk on your own for about one minute. Say where the people are ('They're on a beach, maybe on holiday'), who they are and what they are doing, using the present continuous ('Two girls are jumping', 'Some people are sitting on towels'). Describe details such as clothes, the weather and the sea, and say what you think about the situation ('They look like they're having a lot of fun', 'I think it's very hot because they're wearing shorts and sunglasses'). Useful language: 'In the middle of the photo…', 'Behind them…', 'It seems that…', 'They might be…'. If you don't know a word, describe it in other words ('the thing in the middle that the ball goes over'). Keep talking until the examiner says thank you.

questions.question:
Part 3 (2-3 minutes). Talk to your partner.

Your school is organising a sports day for students of all ages and all levels of fitness. Here are some activities that could be part of the day:

a running race
a tug of war
a basketball competition
a dance class
a table tennis competition
an egg-and-spoon race

Talk together about the different activities, and say which two would be the best for everyone at the school.
questions.explanation: This is a conversation with your partner, not a speech. Talk about the activities one by one, give your opinion with a reason and ask your partner what they think: 'A running race is a bit difficult for students who aren't very fit. What do you think?' Think about the task: the activities must suit everyone, young and old, fit and not so fit. Agree and disagree politely ('You're right, but…', 'I don't really agree because…') and make suggestions ('How about…?', 'What if we…?'). Near the end, try to choose two activities together: 'So, shall we choose the tug of war and the egg-and-spoon race?' The examiner assesses how well you keep the conversation going and respond to your partner.

questions.question:
Part 4 (about 3 minutes). The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about keeping fit and healthy.

What do you do to keep fit?
Do you think young people do enough exercise these days? Why / Why not?
Is it better to do sport alone or with other people? Why?
What can people do to have a healthy diet?
Should schools have more sport lessons? Why / Why not?
questions.explanation: Give full answers with reasons and examples, and react to what your partner says ('I agree with you, because…', 'That's true, but…'). For example: 'I don't think young people do enough exercise, because many of them spend hours on their phones instead of going outside.' Use phrases for opinions ('In my opinion…', 'I believe that…', 'On the other hand…') and 'should' for advice ('People should eat more fruit and vegetables'). The examiner assesses range of language, extending answers and interaction with your partner.

questions.question: When is Harry's new dentist appointment?
options: a) Tuesday afternoon
b) Thursday afternoon
c) Monday morning
questions.explanation: The receptionist says "we've put him in on Thursday at a quarter past four instead". Tuesday afternoon was the old appointment, and Monday morning is not possible because "Harry's at school then".

questions.question: What does the doctor tell Mr Hughes to do?
options: a) Do some exercises
b) Take some tablets
c) Rest his knee on a chair
questions.explanation: The doctor gives him "a sheet with some simple exercises to do three times a day". She says "No, not at all" when he asks about keeping his leg up, and about painkillers she says "try not to".

questions.question: How will Laura travel to the hospital?
options: a) By bus
b) By taxi
c) In Sam's car
questions.explanation: Laura says "The number fourteen bus stops right outside the hospital" and "I'll just leave a bit early". She refuses Sam's offer because he's working, and the bus is "much cheaper than a taxi".

questions.question: Why has Ella come to see the doctor?
options: a) Her throat is sore.
b) Her wrist hurts.
c) Her ear hurts.
questions.explanation: Ella says "The problem is my ear. It's been really painful since Sunday". Her wrist is "fine now", and she answers "No, nothing like that" when asked about a sore throat.

questions.question: Why is Peter Brown phoning the surgery?
options: a) To get his test results
b) To cancel his appointment
c) To move his appointment
questions.explanation: Peter asks "Is there anything on Monday instead?" because he has to work on Friday. He says "I don't want to cancel it completely", and he wants to discuss his test results with Dr Shah at the appointment, not on the phone.

questions.question: Which room does Anna need to go to?
options: a) Room 12 on the second floor
b) Room 8 on the first floor
c) Room 3 on the ground floor
questions.explanation: The receptionist says the nurse is "upstairs today, on the first floor, in Room Eight". Room Three is "being painted this week", and Room Twelve is the doctor's room, "so don't go up that far".

questions.question: What does the dentist tell Ryan to do?
options: a) Eat fewer sweets
b) Come back in six months
c) Brush his teeth for longer
questions.explanation: The dentist says "Try to spend two minutes on it, not thirty seconds." She is happy that he's "not eating too many sweets", and she will see him "in a year", not in six months.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a film they have just seen. What did Aaron think of it?
options: a) It was much too long.
b) The story was hard to follow.
c) The ending was disappointing.
questions.explanation: Aaron says "the last five minutes were so silly" and "I expected something much cleverer." It was Lauren who "got a bit lost"; Aaron thought "it was clear enough", and the two and a half hours "went really quickly".

questions.question: You will hear a girl telling a friend about a concert. How did she feel at the concert?
options: a) Uncomfortable in the crowd
b) Disappointed with the band
c) Too far away from the stage
questions.explanation: Freya says "There were so many people that I couldn't move, and it was so hot" and she was "worrying about getting out". She thought "The band were fantastic", and she never complains that she couldn't see the stage.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a TV talent show. What do they agree about?
options: a) The show is on too late.
b) The judges are unkind.
c) The singers have improved this year.
questions.explanation: Jordan complains about the judges and Molly says "that was horrible. They didn’t need to laugh at him"; Jordan answers "Exactly." Only Molly thinks the singers are better; Jordan says "last year’s were just as good". Nobody mentions the time of the show.

questions.question: You will hear a boy talking about the guitar. Why did he start learning it?
options: a) He wanted to join a band.
b) It was part of his music lessons at school.
c) His parents wanted him to learn.
questions.explanation: Noah says the band "needed a guitarist. I really wanted to be in it, so I asked for lessons". His parents wanted him to learn "the piano", not the guitar, and music at school is "only singing".

questions.question: You will hear a woman and a man deciding what show to see. What do they decide?
options: a) To see a musical
b) To go to a comedy night
c) To watch a dance show
questions.explanation: Neil says "I've never seen modern dance. Let's try something new" and Sara agrees: "Great, I'll book it." Neil is "not a big fan of musicals", and the comedy night is "sold out".

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a music festival. What is Tyler's attitude to going?
options: a) He doesn't like the bands.
b) He isn't sure he has enough money.
c) He is excited about camping there.
questions.explanation: Tyler mentions the cost ("ninety pounds, plus the train"), says "I'm saving for a laptop" and "I'll see how much I've got at the end of the month." He says "The bands are great this year", and "sleeping in a tent isn't my favourite thing".

questions.question: The club meets every ____.
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says 'the club will meet every Thursday'. Wednesday is on the poster, but she says 'that's a mistake'.

questions.question: Place: the new kitchen behind the ____
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says 'We'll be using the new kitchen behind the sports hall, not the old classroom near the library'. The library is near the old classroom, which is too small.

questions.question: Cost: ____ pounds a week, which pays for the ingredients.
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says 'The club costs two pounds a week. That money pays for all the ingredients'.

questions.question: In the first session, students will make ____.
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says they 'were planning to make pizza', but because an oven is being repaired, 'instead we'll be making soup'. Pizza will come later in the term.

questions.question: Bring a ____ with a lid to take your food home in.
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says 'please bring a plastic box with a lid each week, so that you can take home whatever you've made'. Aprons are provided, so students do not need to bring one.

questions.question: End of term: a ____ judged by the head teacher.
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says 'at the end of term, we'll hold a competition, and our head teacher has kindly agreed to be the judge'.

questions.question: What was Owen's main reason for doing the trip?
options: a) His cousin persuaded him to go with him.
b) He needed a complete change from studying.
c) He wanted to raise money for a hospital.
questions.explanation: Owen says he had spent the year 'revising for exams' and 'was desperate to do something physical, something completely different.' He collected some money for a hospital, 'but that wasn't the main reason', and his cousin simply 'felt the same'.

questions.question: How does Owen feel now about the planning they did?
options: a) He is glad they organised everything carefully.
b) He thinks they planned too much.
c) He wishes they had prepared their route better.
questions.explanation: Owen says they did 'Far too much' planning and 'Looking back, that was a mistake.' He is not glad about it, and he wants to 'leave much more to chance' next time, not prepare more.

questions.question: What did Owen find hardest during the trip?
options: a) Waiting for his cousin to get better
b) Climbing the steep hills on his bike
c) Cycling for days in heavy rain
questions.explanation: Owen says 'the worst thing was when Ben got a stomach bug and we had to stay in a small town for three days. I felt so frustrated'. He says the hills 'were fine', and the wet days only 'weren't much fun'.

questions.question: What does Owen say about the people he met in France?
options: a) They were surprised to see cyclists.
b) Most of them were able to speak good English.
c) They were kinder than he had expected.
questions.explanation: Owen was afraid 'people might be impatient with us', but 'Actually, everyone was incredibly kind.' He says 'Hardly anyone spoke English'.

questions.question: How did Owen feel when they reached the Mediterranean?
options: a) Sorry that the trip was over
b) Excited and keen to celebrate
c) Proud of how fit he had become
questions.explanation: Owen says 'I felt a bit sad more than anything' because 'suddenly it was over.' He had imagined 'jumping up and down, celebrating', but that is not how he actually felt.

questions.question: What does Owen say about doing a trip like this?
options: a) It's worth paying for a really good bike.
b) It is more fun to travel on your own.
c) You can do it without being very fit.
questions.explanation: Owen says 'People think you need to be really fit before you start, but we weren't' and 'You get fitter every day.' His own bike was 'second-hand', and he advises going 'with someone you get on well with', not alone.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) You have to pay £1 every time you open your locker.
b) You can buy a locker key at reception for £15.
c) You get your £1 back when you unlock the locker.
questions.explanation: The sign says 'Your coin will come back to you when you open it again', so using a locker costs nothing in the end. You do not pay each time you open it, and £15 is what it costs if you lose a key, not the price of buying one.

questions.question: Why has Coach Dan written this message?
options: a) To tell parents about a change of day
b) To invite parents to watch a competition
c) To say that this week's training is cancelled
questions.explanation: Dan explains that 'our training session is moving to Sunday at the same time', so the day has changed. Training is not cancelled, it is moved, and the competition is only the reason the pool is closed – he does not invite anyone to it.

questions.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) The fast lane is only open for thirty minutes at a time.
b) Swimmers have to pass a speed test before using the fast lane.
c) Slower swimmers in the fast lane should change lanes.
questions.explanation: The notice says 'If other swimmers are often passing you, please move to the medium lane', so slower swimmers should change lanes. Nobody has to take a test, and '30 seconds' is the time for 25 metres, not how long the lane is open.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) A nine-year-old should not change in this room.
b) Young children must change with a parent of the same sex.
c) Adults without children may also use this room.
questions.explanation: 'Children aged 8 and over must use the male or female changing rooms', so a nine-year-old cannot use the family room. The room is 'for adults with children under 8 only', so adults on their own cannot use it, and the sign says nothing about young children changing with a parent of the same sex.

questions.question: What is the leisure centre telling members?
options: a) Members will be given a free cap in March.
b) Some swimmers will need to wear a cap from March.
c) Every swimmer must buy a cap at reception.
questions.explanation: Only 'swimmers with hair longer than their shoulders must wear a swimming cap' from 1 March, so the rule is for some swimmers. Caps are not free – they cost '£3' – and nobody has to buy one at reception because 'you are welcome to bring your own'.

questions.question: Carlos is going to Japan next spring and wants to learn some useful Japanese first. He only has about ten minutes a day, and he is most worried about speaking.
options: A) FitPro Coach
B) WildSpotter
C) TalkTrip
D) BasketWise
E) FocusDesk
F) LinguaBite
G) StrideTrack
H) MealMap
questions.explanation: TalkTrip has 'ten-minute daily lessons in Japanese', and 'The app listens as you repeat each phrase out loud and tells you how to improve your pronunciation', which helps his speaking. LinguaBite also teaches Japanese in short lessons, but it only has 'reading and writing exercises'.

questions.question: Fiona wants to spend less on food for her family by planning the week's meals in advance. She'd like her husband and children to be able to add things to the shopping list too.
options: A) FitPro Coach
B) WildSpotter
C) TalkTrip
D) BasketWise
E) FocusDesk
F) LinguaBite
G) StrideTrack
H) MealMap
questions.explanation: With MealMap you 'Choose your meals for the week', it 'suggests cheaper recipes', and 'Everyone in the family can add items to the same list from their own phone'. BasketWise also helps you save money, but it does not plan meals and the list is only 'saved on your phone'.

questions.question: Jamal has just started running and wants an app that records his runs. He'd like to compete with his friends, but he doesn't want to pay anything.
options: A) FitPro Coach
B) WildSpotter
C) TalkTrip
D) BasketWise
E) FocusDesk
F) LinguaBite
G) StrideTrack
H) MealMap
questions.explanation: StrideTrack 'is completely free', 'records your distance, speed and route', and sets 'challenges for your group' so friends can 'see who can run the furthest'. FitPro Coach also records runs and lets you compare results with friends, but after the free trial it 'costs £4.99 a month'.

questions.question: Ellen goes walking in the hills every weekend and often sees plants and birds she doesn't know the names of. There's usually no mobile signal where she walks.
options: A) FitPro Coach
B) WildSpotter
C) TalkTrip
D) BasketWise
E) FocusDesk
F) LinguaBite
G) StrideTrack
H) MealMap
questions.explanation: WildSpotter tells you what 'a flower, tree or bird' is from a photo, and 'the app will work perfectly even where there is no phone signal'. StrideTrack also works 'with no phone signal', but it only records runs and cannot tell her the names of plants or birds.

questions.question: Kofi has important exams in June, but he keeps looking at social media instead of studying. He also needs help organising his revision so that he covers every subject.
options: A) FitPro Coach
B) WildSpotter
C) TalkTrip
D) BasketWise
E) FocusDesk
F) LinguaBite
G) StrideTrack
H) MealMap
questions.explanation: FocusDesk 'blocks social media and games' and, when you give it your exam dates and subjects, 'it will create a revision timetable for you'. LinguaBite also 'builds a personal study plan', but only for language lessons, and it does not stop him using social media.

questions.question: Why does Daniel mention that his host family spoke excellent English?
options: a) It was the main reason he decided to go to Norway.
b) It made it easy for him to avoid learning Norwegian.
c) It meant that he could follow his lessons at school.
d) It helped him to make friends at school quickly.
questions.explanation: Daniel says their English 'was a relief at first. The problem was that I used it as an excuse. For the first two months I hardly learnt any Norwegian.' He could not follow lessons ('lessons I couldn't follow'), and he chose Norway 'because of the mountains in the photos', not because of the family's English.

questions.question: How did Even help Daniel when he was feeling lonely?
options: a) He gave him some useful advice about feeling homesick.
b) He translated the instructions for him at training.
c) He taught him how to play handball before school.
d) He got him into a team where nobody spoke English.
questions.explanation: "He didn’t give me any advice. Instead, he asked me to join his handball team… Nobody spoke English during training, so I had no choice." Even did not translate; Daniel "had to understand the instructions" himself. There is no mention of Even teaching him the game at home or before school.

questions.question: What did Daniel think of his Norwegian school at first?
options: a) He thought the teachers were very strict.
b) He preferred it to his school in England.
c) He was not sure what he was supposed to do.
d) He found the tests there much too difficult.
questions.explanation: He writes: 'At first I found this confusing. Nobody told me exactly what to do.' The 'lots of homework and tests' were in England, not Norway, and students used teachers' first names, which does not suggest strict teachers. He only saw the benefit later, so he did not prefer it at first.

questions.question: How did Daniel feel when he got back to England?
options: a) Excited to tell his old friends all about Norway
b) Relieved that a difficult year was finally over
c) As if he did not really belong there any more
d) Pleased to be back with his friends again
questions.explanation: 'Back in England I felt strangely out of place for months. My old friends had moved on.' He had 'expected to be excited about going home', but he was not, and his friends were not interested in his stories, so he was not pleased or relieved.

questions.question: What is Daniel's main purpose in writing this text?
options: a) To show that a hard experience can still be worth it
b) To persuade more teachers to organise school exchanges
c) To explain how to learn a foreign language quickly
d) To compare school life in England and in Norway
questions.explanation: He tells his students to go but warns 'it won't be what they expect', and ends: 'the more important lesson was that feeling uncomfortable is often the first step towards something good.' Schools and language learning are only parts of his story, and he does not ask teachers to organise exchanges.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (1)?
options: A) Using a phone in bed, for example, can make it much harder to fall asleep.
B) 'Adults only see us staring at a screen,' she says, 'not what we're actually doing.'
C) The study also found that most teenagers watch less television than their parents did.
D) Much of that time, they point out, is spent doing several things at once.
E) As a result, she has decided to delete all the social media apps on her phone.
F) But how many hours do teenagers really spend in front of them?
G) Sleep experts say that teenagers need at least eight hours of sleep every night.
H) At first, a lot of them were angry about the new rule.
questions.explanation: 'Them' refers to the screens listed before ('Phones, tablets, games consoles'), and the question 'how many hours do teenagers really spend' is answered by the next sentence: 'the average is around seven hours a day'. The sentence about the study also finding something cannot fit, because the study has not been mentioned yet.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (2)?
options: A) Using a phone in bed, for example, can make it much harder to fall asleep.
B) 'Adults only see us staring at a screen,' she says, 'not what we're actually doing.'
C) The study also found that most teenagers watch less television than their parents did.
D) Much of that time, they point out, is spent doing several things at once.
E) As a result, she has decided to delete all the social media apps on her phone.
F) But how many hours do teenagers really spend in front of them?
G) Sleep experts say that teenagers need at least eight hours of sleep every night.
H) At first, a lot of them were angry about the new rule.
questions.explanation: 'They' refers to the 'researchers', 'that time' to the seven hours, and 'doing several things at once' is explained by the next sentence: a teenager might be 'listening to music, chatting to friends and watching a video at the same moment'. The sentence about television does not explain why the number should be treated carefully.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (3)?
options: A) Using a phone in bed, for example, can make it much harder to fall asleep.
B) 'Adults only see us staring at a screen,' she says, 'not what we're actually doing.'
C) The study also found that most teenagers watch less television than their parents did.
D) Much of that time, they point out, is spent doing several things at once.
E) As a result, she has decided to delete all the social media apps on her phone.
F) But how many hours do teenagers really spend in front of them?
G) Sleep experts say that teenagers need at least eight hours of sleep every night.
H) At first, a lot of them were angry about the new rule.
questions.explanation: Dr Ward thinks the problem is 'when', and using a phone 'in bed' is an example ('for example') of the wrong time. 'The bright light' in the next sentence is the light from that phone. The sentence about needing eight hours of sleep does not mention a screen, so 'The bright light' would have nothing to refer to.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (4)?
options: A) Using a phone in bed, for example, can make it much harder to fall asleep.
B) 'Adults only see us staring at a screen,' she says, 'not what we're actually doing.'
C) The study also found that most teenagers watch less television than their parents did.
D) Much of that time, they point out, is spent doing several things at once.
E) As a result, she has decided to delete all the social media apps on her phone.
F) But how many hours do teenagers really spend in front of them?
G) Sleep experts say that teenagers need at least eight hours of sleep every night.
H) At first, a lot of them were angry about the new rule.
questions.explanation: 'Them' refers to the 'students' who hand in their phones, 'the new rule' to that arrangement, and 'At first' contrasts with the next sentence: 'Now… most of them say they prefer it'. No other sentence prepares the change of opinion shown by 'Now'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (5)?
options: A) Using a phone in bed, for example, can make it much harder to fall asleep.
B) 'Adults only see us staring at a screen,' she says, 'not what we're actually doing.'
C) The study also found that most teenagers watch less television than their parents did.
D) Much of that time, they point out, is spent doing several things at once.
E) As a result, she has decided to delete all the social media apps on her phone.
F) But how many hours do teenagers really spend in front of them?
G) Sleep experts say that teenagers need at least eight hours of sleep every night.
H) At first, a lot of them were angry about the new rule.
questions.explanation: Maya explains that she uses her phone to keep 'in touch with her cousins' and to learn the guitar, and her words 'Adults only see us staring at a screen' repeat the idea that teenagers are 'not always happy with the way adults talk about the subject'. The sentence about her deleting her social media apps contradicts her defence of her phone.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (1).
options: a) worried
b) afraid
c) anxious
d) upset
questions.explanation: The pattern is "afraid of" something: the writer says "I'm afraid of heights". 'Worried' and 'anxious' are followed by 'about', not 'of', and 'upset of' is not possible.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (2).
options: a) got
b) did
c) took
d) made
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "make sure": Dan "made sure that we understood the safety rules", meaning he checked it. 'Did sure', 'took sure' and 'got sure' are not English.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (3).
options: a) level
b) height
c) size
d) step
questions.explanation: We talk about "a level of difficulty": each colour showed how hard the route was, from "the easy yellow route" upwards. 'Height', 'size' and 'step of difficulty' are not used in English.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (4).
options: a) give
b) stop
c) end
d) leave
questions.explanation: Dan wants the writer to keep climbing: "Don't give up now - you're nearly there!" 'Give up' means stop trying. 'Stop up', 'end up' and 'leave up' do not have this meaning ('end up' means 'finally be somewhere').

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (5).
options: a) made
b) had
c) taken
d) done
questions.explanation: The collocation is "have fun", so in the past perfect it is "I had had a lot of fun". We do not say 'do fun', 'make fun' (which means laughing at someone unkindly, and needs 'of') or 'take fun'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (6).
options: a) spent
b) charged
c) booked
d) paid
questions.explanation: They "have already booked another session for next Saturday", meaning they have arranged it in advance. 'Paid' would need 'for' (paid for a session), 'spent a session' refers to time already used, and 'charged' is what the centre does to customers.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the relative pronoun for possession: "a woman whose family had come to England" means 'a woman, and her family had come to England'. 'Who' or 'that' cannot be followed directly by a noun like 'family' in this way.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: 'By + reflexive pronoun' means 'alone': "she lives by herself", while her sons only "visit her every weekend". The subject is 'she', so the reflexive pronoun must be 'herself'.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: Ines has "two grown-up sons", and 'both of them' refers to two people together: "Both of them play in a jazz band". 'All' is used for three or more, and 'neither' does not fit because she says it "proudly" and the verb is positive.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: A past simple question needs the auxiliary 'did': "Where did you live before?" The word 'before' and the answer about a flat she no longer lives in show the past, so 'do' is wrong.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (5).
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'turn out that' means 'it was discovered that': "It soon turned out that Ines was a piano teacher".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'get on (well) with someone', meaning have a friendly relationship: "she gets on well with everyone in our building".

questions.question:
Part 1. You must answer this question.

Read this email from your neighbour, Mrs Hughes, and the notes you have made.

From: Carol Hughes
Subject: Could you help us?

Hello,

We're going to visit my sister in Scotland from 3 to 10 August. Would you be able to look after our cat, Biscuit, while we're away? [Note 1: Yes, …]

Biscuit needs food twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening. What time would be best for you to come round? [Note 2: Tell Mrs Hughes]

Is there anything you would like to know about looking after her? [Note 3: Ask about …]

We'd like to thank you for your help. Is there anything we could bring you back from Scotland? [Note 4: Explain]

Best wishes,
Carol Hughes

Write your email to Mrs Hughes using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: A good answer is a polite but friendly email to a neighbour (e.g. 'Dear Mrs Hughes,' … 'Best wishes,') of about 100 words that deals with all four notes: (1) agrees to look after the cat ('Yes, of course, I'd be happy to look after Biscuit'); (2) says what times suit the writer ('I could come at about 8 a.m. before school and at 6 p.m.'); (3) asks a question about looking after Biscuit ('Does she need any medicine?' / 'Can I let her go outside?'); (4) explains what the writer would like, or that nothing is needed ('You don't need to bring me anything, but some Scottish chocolate would be lovely!'). Marks are given for Content (all four notes), Communicative Achievement (a polite tone suitable for an adult neighbour), Organisation (paragraphs and linking words) and Language (B1 structures such as 'I'd be happy to…', 'Could you tell me…?', indirect questions). Missing a note reduces the Content mark.

questions.question:
Part 2. Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2: Article
You see this notice in an English-language magazine.

ARTICLES WANTED!
Why animals are important to people
Why do people keep pets? How can animals help people in their lives? Is there an animal that is important to you?
Write an article answering these questions. We will publish the most interesting articles.

Write your article.

Question 3: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
'The dog would not stop barking.'

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Candidates answer only ONE question, in about 100 words.
